newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Unilever focus is on Israeli market.
newsitem.headline: Unilever focus is on Israeli market.

text.p: Unilever PLC has set its sights first on serving the local market in its 18-month-old drive to establish a major presence in Israel, the company's Israel chairman Ray Bremner said on Thursday.
If Unilever does decide to use its Israeli operations to serve foreign markets, they will be in Europe and the United States -- not the Middle East, he said.
"One of the advantages of the peace process is the opening up of the Western market to Israeli business, which has much higher potential than the Middle East," Bremner told Reuters.
"Although everyone talks about the peace process opening up the Middle East, it has really opened up the world," he said.

Unilever acquired a 50 percent stake in the ice cream business of Strauss Dairies in September 1995 and in April 1996 acquired 60 percent of Witco, a maker of of detergents and personal care products whose name has since been changed to Lever Israel.
Earlier this week Kedem Chemicals Ltd said it was in talks with the Anglo-Dutch company to form a joint venture in the field of industrial cleaning and related materials.

Bremner said Unilever was eyeing other acquisitions but was not negotiating any deals yet. He denied newspaper reports that it was holding talks with Careline, a cosmetics and personal-care products maker controlled by Agis Industries Ltd.
Bremner, who arrived in Israel in May 1996 after a stint in Dubai, said that ultimately Unilever wants to have Israeli businesses in food, personal care products and industrial chemicals.
"In areas specific to one category there will be one company," he said.

In the last two years there have been a string of acqusitions by multinationals in Israel. Nestle SA took a 40 percent stake in Osem Investments Ltd last year and Donone's bought a 20 percent stake in Strauss' other dairy operations earlier this month.
Bremner said Unilever was not wholly committed to buying more Israeli companies and was watching competitors who are relying on importers to market their products here.
"We can grow from the businesses acquired or we can seek growth from acquisitions," he said.
Bremner said Unilever's Israeli businesses could one day be exporting to Europe and the United States. But he said, the company first had to get costs down and raise quality standards.
"Our challenge is to put in world class technology and quality," he said.
